syllabusRef: Investigative Study (AAC section of the specification, Descriptors of Quality)

notes.h: What the Investigative Study is and how it is weighted
notes.b: The Business Alive Investigative Study is a student-led research report written in response to a brief set by the SEC (State Examinations Commission). It is the additional assessment component (AAC) of Leaving Certificate Business, so it sits alongside the written exam rather than inside it.
points: The study asks you to conduct, analyse and evaluate research on a particular issue, using a variety of sources and considering a range of perspectives, while drawing on your ongoing engagement with the world of business.
It is worth 40% of the overall marks, which is 200 marks, and the written examination is worth the remaining 60%. Keep the two apart: the study is the AAC, the exam is the written paper.
One common brief is set for Higher and Ordinary Level, so every student answers the same brief, and the study is assessed at the level at which you sit the final examination.
The SEC issues the brief in term two of 5th year, the study takes up to 20 hours, and the report is submitted digitally during 6th year as an individual report.
Per the 2027 SEC brief, work is completed and given to the class teacher by 12 March 2027. Check the date in the brief itself in case it changes.
The 2027 brief allocates the 200 marks as: Introduction 20, Investigation, Findings, Analysis and Evaluation 100, Conclusion 30, and Overall Coherence 50. Confirm these figures in the brief.
Overall Coherence is a 50-mark award for the whole report, not a section of it. This is why it is easy to confuse with the Conclusion, which is a section worth 30.

The NCCA Descriptors of Quality (planning, investigating, applying and communicating) describe high, moderate and low achievement across the work. They are not a mark scheme: the marks come from the SEC brief's allocation.
notes.tip: Examiners and exam questions can ask you to outline the requirements of the study. Keep the confusable pairs clear: the study (40%) versus the written exam (60%), and Overall Coherence (a mark for the whole report) versus the Conclusion (a section).

notes.b: The 2027 SEC brief sets the limits and the layout, and the NCCA guidelines say such instructions cover things like the word count and number of images. There is no SEC template, so structuring the document is your own responsibility.
points: The report body is no more than 1,500 words. Going over the limit is a common mistake, and the brief rewards skilful brevity, so a tight question helps you stay inside it.
References, data tables, graphs, diagrams, images and labels do not count towards the 1,500 words, so use graphics to present data clearly rather than spending words on it.
No more than 10 images may be used in the whole report. Images must not be used to carry extra text, and any image you refer to is labelled Figure 1, Figure 2 and so on.
Headings are Arial, black, size 14 and bold. Body text is Arial, black, size 12 with 1.5 line spacing, so coloured or highlighted text and other fonts are not allowed.
Pages are portrait with page numbers at the bottom centre and 20 mm margins on all sides, with nothing written in the margins.
The completed SEC cover page is the first page, and the report is submitted as a PDF. Print it and proof-read the printed copy first, so that you catch anything that does not show up as you intended.
notes.tip: A common mistake is going over the word count or putting extra text into an image. If asked to identify and explain a formatting or length rule, name the rule from the 2027 brief and say why it matters, for example that the limit forces brevity and focus.

notes.b: The 2027 SEC brief sets five headings, each starting on a new page. The suggested word counts for the first four add up to the 1,500-word limit, and the References are not counted.
points: Section 1, Introduction (about 200 words): the research question, your rationale for choosing it, and reflection on how you engaged with the project plan.
Section 2, Investigation and Findings (about 400 words): the purpose and relevance of the research methods and sources you used, and the findings presented from a variety of perspectives.
Section 3, Analysis and Evaluation (about 600 words): in-depth analysis and evaluation of the data, showing originality and critical thinking, with the limitations of the study identified.

Section 4, Conclusions (about 300 words): conclusions justified by the analysis, how planning contributed to completing the study, how your perspective evolved, and links to the real world of business.
Section 5, References: every source used, including any AI tool, set out so a reader can trace it. The References are not counted in the word limit.
There is no separate project-plan section. Because the plan is not submitted, your planning is shown through reflection in the Introduction and Conclusions and throughout the report.
notes.tip: A common mistake is writing a plan section when none is required, or a conclusion that does not answer the question. To show planning, cite specific changes you made to the plan and the effect they had.

notes.h: The six stages of the study
notes.b: The NCCA guidelines set out the study as a learning sequence of six stages. Each stage produces the evidence that the next stage uses, and the timings below are the NCCA's indicative hours.
points: Stage 1, getting started (2-3 hours): read the brief, carry out initial background research and begin an investigative folder.

Stage 2, developing a question (1-2 hours): refine your ideas into one SMART research question (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) with a clear business focus. Discuss it with your teacher; it can be refined further.
Stage 3, project plan (1-2 hours): set objectives, tasks, your role, resources, a time schedule and possible risks, then keep monitoring what is working.

Stage 4, sources and data, together with Stage 5, analysis and evaluation, take 6-8 hours combined. In Stage 4 you gather primary and secondary data, judge each source, and record and acknowledge everything as you go.
Stage 5, analysis and evaluation: interpret the data, evaluate the findings and the different perspectives, and identify the limitations.

Stage 6, applying learning and drawing conclusions (1-2 hours): draw justified conclusions, apply them to the world of business and the cross-cutting themes, and reflect on how your perspective changed. Compiling the final report takes a further 2-3 hours.
Monitoring and reflection run across all six stages, not just at the end, because you cannot reflect honestly on your planning unless you noted what changed as it happened.
notes.tip: If asked to outline or describe the stages, give the stage names in order with one purpose each.

notes.h: The investigative folder and the project plan
notes.b: Both are working tools. Neither is submitted to the SEC, so their value has to show up in the report.
points: The NCCA encourages you to keep an investigative folder that records your thoughts, how they change, your sources and the dates you accessed them. It is encouraged, not required, and it is not submitted.
The project plan is shared with your teacher at intervals as part of ongoing authentication (the process that confirms the work is your own), but only the report is submitted.
You refer to the plan in the report by reflecting on and evaluating it, so it is credited through the Introduction and Conclusions rather than as a section.
Dated notes of problems met and changes made give you specific planning decisions to reflect on, which is far stronger than writing only that a plan was made.
notes.tip: Expect to be asked how a student can show planning when the plan is not submitted: through reflection in the Introduction and Conclusions, citing specific changes made and their effect.

notes.b: The planning descriptor rewards a focused question and planning that you engage with and reflect on throughout. The descriptors describe high, moderate and low achievement in each area.
points: High achievement shows a clear and probing research question, underpinned by why it matters to business locally, nationally or internationally. Moderate achievement is a clear question, and low is some form of question.
High achievement shows effective engagement with planning throughout, with clear reflection on and evaluation of how far the planning helped complete the study.
Writing only that a plan was made is low achievement. The report needs to say what changed in the plan and what effect that had, so keep a record as you go.
notes.tip: A common mistake is stating that you made a plan without saying what changed. Name a specific change and its effect.

notes.b: The investigating descriptor rewards the range of sources and the judgement you apply to them.
points: High achievement identifies and evaluates the potential value of a wide range of appropriate sources, and justifies the choice of each.

Judge each source for relevance, reliability, how recent it is, bias and purpose, and whether it is fact or opinion, and let that judgement show in the report. Describing a source without judging it is a common mistake.
High achievement includes in-depth analysis and evaluation, with conclusions justified by the analysis.

Limitations are clearly identified across the design of the question, the research gathered and the analysis, such as a small sample, a single sector or out-of-date data. State the effect of each limitation too, because a limitation listed without its effect is a common mistake.

notes.b: The applying descriptor rewards relating your findings to the world of business, which is the focus of Stage 6.
points: High achievement reflects on how the findings relate to business, and to business stories in the media where relevant, and on how your perspective was influenced by the findings.
Findings are clearly related to the cross-cutting themes of the specification, such as ethics, sustainability and digital, with the link explained rather than just listed.
The 2027 topic is itself about digital technology in work, so the digital theme fits naturally, and you can add an ethical angle such as employee privacy.
Conclusions are justified by the analysis and answer the research question directly. A conclusion that does not answer the question is a common mistake.
notes.tip: Another common mistake is no link to business or the media. Relate each finding back to the world of business and say how it changed your view.

notes.b: The communicating descriptor rewards a clear, coherent report that is fully referenced.
points: High achievement presents data, information and analysis clearly, using a range of relevant graphics that are labelled and referred to in the text. A graph that is unlabelled or not mentioned in the text is a common mistake.
Language is coherent and consistent throughout, and uses correct business terms, so choose the precise term rather than an everyday phrase.

References are clear and complete: every in-text citation links to an entry in the reference list, with enough detail to find the source and the date an online source was accessed. No formal referencing style is required.
Reflections on the study are part of the descriptor, so the report should show what you learned, not only what you found.

notes.h: The 2027 topic: a digital work practice
notes.b: The 2027 brief asks you to investigate how a work practice that uses digital technology is impacting either employers or employees, supported by primary and/or secondary data. State the topic loosely and check the exact wording in the SEC brief.
points: A digital work practice is a way of working that relies on digital tools, such as video calls for meetings, a shared cloud drive for files, remote working or an online scheduling app.
A digital work practice is not digital technology in general, and it need not be remote working: remote working is only one example.
The topic concerns the impact on employers or on employees. A narrower study is easier to answer well, so pick one side, and check in the brief whether you must choose one.

Impacts on employers include costs, productivity, recruitment and security of data. Impacts on employees include flexibility, workload, skills needs, wellbeing and the right to disconnect (not being expected to work outside normal hours).
A strong study narrows to one practice and one affected group, so that the research question stays answerable within 1,500 words using primary and/or secondary data.

A sample question could look at how video meetings affect employee workload, using a short survey (primary data) and a published report (secondary data). This is a sample business topic, not a model report.
notes.tip: A common mistake is studying employers and employees both, which makes the question too broad for 1,500 words. Do not assume the topic must be remote working.

notes.h: Irish examples to apply to the topic
notes.b: Two Irish developments show how a digital work practice affects employers and employees. Use them as examples to support a discussion, not as a substitute for your own research.
points: The right to request remote working came into operation on 7 March 2024 under the Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023, and it applies to all employees. The right to request flexible working applies to parents and carers.
The Code of Practice for these requests was made by S.I. No. 92/2024. For employees it is a route to flexibility, and for employers it means handling such requests.

The WRC Code of Practice on the Right to Disconnect took effect on 1 April 2021. It covers an employee's right not to routinely work outside normal hours, a right not to be penalised for refusing, and a duty to respect colleagues' right to disconnect.
Failure to follow the right to disconnect code is not an offence, but it can be used as evidence before the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) or the Labour Court.
The CSO reported for Q4 2025 that about 957,000 people work from home. This comes from the Labour Force Survey, and the figure may be revised.
To use an example in an answer: state the fact, link it to employers or employees, give one benefit and one drawback, and finish with a judgement that includes an ethical or digital angle.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate or discuss a digital work practice, give one benefit and one drawback for employers or for employees, each developed, then a justified judgement. You can link to the right to request remote working or the right to disconnect.

notes.h: Ethics, sustainability and entrepreneurial thinking in the study
notes.b: The cross-cutting themes are not just for the written paper. The way you carry out the study can show them, and your report can discuss them.
points: Ethics: use honest data, get consent from anyone you interview, submit your own work, and acknowledge any AI you use.
Digital: the 2027 brief is itself about digital technology at work, so you can discuss data security and the monitoring of employees. AI tools can be wrong or biased, so check what they tell you.
Sustainability: remote working reduces commuting, and digital working uses energy. Treat these as qualitative points and do not state figures you have not checked.
Entrepreneurial thinking: apply the planning, risk and adaptation mindset to the study itself by spotting risks early and changing the plan when something goes wrong.

notes.b: The work must be your own, and every source you use must be acknowledged.
points: Authentication is a process that runs across the study, with the teacher seeing the plan and work in progress. The student, teacher and school confirm as the brief instructs that the work is the student's own.
Teachers should not engage in corrections of the report for redrafting by the student. A teacher may discuss your proposed question with you at the question stage.

Any use of AI must be acknowledged in the references with the tool name, the date, how it was used, and the share link if the tool gives one, or otherwise the prompt. An unacknowledged AI output is a common mistake.

Submitting work that is not entirely completed by you is a significant breach of regulations, and penalties can include withholding of the related results. This is why you should reference every source as you work.
notes.tip: Remember the common mistake of unacknowledged AI use. Record the tool, date, use and prompt or share link as you go.

keyTerms.definition: A student-led research report on a business question set by an SEC brief, worth 40% of Leaving Certificate Business.
The NCCA descriptions of high, moderate and low achievement in planning, investigating, applying and communicating.
The 50 marks the 2027 SEC brief awards for the report as a whole, not a section; the communicating descriptor rewards coherent, consistent language, clear graphics and acknowledged references.
The focused question the study sets out to answer, tested against SMART criteria before data collection begins.
A record of the student's thoughts, sources and changes during the study, which is encouraged but not submitted to the SEC.
The process by which the student, teacher and school confirm, as the SEC brief instructs, that the submitted work is the student's own.
A way of doing work that depends on digital tools, such as video calls or shared cloud files.
Recording and crediting every source used, including any AI tool with its name, date and how it was used, within the report.
1,500 words in the 2027 SEC brief, not counting references, data tables, graphs, diagrams, images or labels.

questions.prompt: Explain what the investigating descriptor rewards, and describe what high achievement looks like for a study of a digital work practice.
questions.model: The investigating descriptor rewards the range of sources used and the judgement applied to them. High achievement identifies and evaluates the potential value of a wide range of appropriate sources, such as a survey of employees, an interview with a manager and an independent report on the practice, and justifies why each was chosen. Each source is judged for relevance, reliability, how recent it is, bias and purpose, and this judgement is visible in the report rather than assumed. Limitations are clearly identified across the question, the research and the analysis, for example a small survey sample drawn from one workplace.

questions.prompt: The project plan is not submitted with the Investigative Study. Explain how a student can still earn credit for planning.
questions.model: Planning is rewarded through the report itself. The Introduction must reflect on how the student engaged with the project plan, and the Conclusions must outline how planning contributed to completing the study, so the student should keep dated notes of problems met and changes made, such as changing a survey after a low response rate. Sharing the plan with the teacher during the study supports authentication, but the marks depend on specific, honest reflection written into the report.

questions.prompt: State two rules on formatting that a student must follow in the report, and explain why each matters.
questions.model: The report body must be no more than 1,500 words, which requires a word budget for each section so that the report stays focused; going over may lose marks. The report must be converted to a PDF that is printed and proof-read, with nothing in the 20 mm margins, because anything that is not visible on the printed copy cannot be seen by the examiner and earns no marks.
